prose.article: προφθάνω means to get ahead of someone, anticipating their action by doing or saying something first. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 17:25, where Jesus speaks before Peter can, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "preempted." In the Septuagint it occurs 17 times, mostly translating Hebrew קָדַם ("to come before, meet"), and a papyrus from 161 B.C. uses it of a man who got to the temple door first and shut it before others could reach him.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its precise New Testament shade of meaning rests on a single verse.

issues: Syntactic role data flags 'vocative (1×)' which is anomalous for a finite verb and may reflect a tagging artifact, but the definition does not acknowledge any ambiguity in how the word functions syntactically at MAT 17:25

The KJV gloss 'prevent' (in its archaic English sense of 'come before') is historically significant for Bible readers and is omitted from the article, which could confuse readers encountering older translations

The definition phrase 'speaking or moving first' adds 'moving first' as a generalization not directly supported by the single NT occurrence, which concerns speaking; the papyrus example concerns physical action but that is extra-NT evidence

The supporting article is accurate but the definition itself is slightly over-specified by the phrase 'getting ahead of them by speaking or moving first' — the core meaning is simply to anticipate or act before another, without restriction to speech or movement

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence shows Jesus anticipating Peter's report by speaking first, directly demonstrating the 'act before someone else' meaning the definition captures.
The KJV renders this verse with 'prevent' in its archaic sense of 'come before,' a gloss the article omits, which could mislead readers of older English translations who expect a warning sense.

why: προχειρίζομαι occurs 3 times in the Byzantine (Majority) New Testament, across 1 book.

The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “appointed” in 2 of those places (67%), e.g. Acts 3:20; Acts 22:14. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 100% of the same verses.
In the Septuagint it appears 3 times, most often translating the Hebrew בִּי (H994) (1×).
Moulton–Milligan documents this word in everyday papyri and inscriptions, anchoring the meaning in ordinary Koine usage outside the New Testament.
Low confidence: very few occurrences; lexicon definitions carry more weight than corpus statistics here.

prose.def: To choose someone in advance for a task or role; to appoint, designate, or select beforehand.
prose.article: This verb means to pick someone out ahead of time for a particular purpose, and in its 3 New Testament occurrences (all in Acts) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "appointed" twice. The everyday Greek of the papyri confirms this strongly: documents speak of "appointed collectors" of taxes and officials "appointed" to receive and transmit records, showing it was an ordinary administrative word for designating someone to a job. Built from "before" (pró) and a derivative of "hand" (cheír), it literally suggests taking something into one's hand in advance, which Strong's and Abbott-Smith connect to the figurative sense of purposing or choosing.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin (only 3 occurrences, all in Acts) and the rendering data and lexicons divide it differently, so the exact shading is uncertain.

issues: Sense 2 label 'appeared appoint what' is garbled and unintelligible as a sense label

Abbott-Smith distinguishes two distinct senses: (1) passive 'to put into the hand, deliver up' (ACT 3:20) and (2) middle deponent 'to choose/appoint' (ACT 22:14, ACT 26:16); the current definition collapses this distinction

The definition focuses only on choosing 'someone' but ACT 26:16 uses it with accusative of persons while ACT 22:14 uses it with an infinitive, showing the object can be a purpose/action, not just a person
The definition does not acknowledge the passive voice sense attested at ACT 3:20 where Jesus is the one delivered up/appointed, which differs semantically from the active choosing sense
Syntactic role data lists 'vocative (3×)' which appears to be a data error (the word is a verb, not a noun in direct address) and the definition does not help readers navigate this anomaly

receipts.how: Paul is told God 'appointed' him to know his will and see the Righteous One, fitting the core definition of purposeful advance designation.
Christ tells Paul he has been chosen for a role, corroborating the 'appoint/choose' sense but with accusative of person, showing the object is a person, not just a task.
Abbott-Smith reads this as the passive sense 'put into the hand / delivered up' referring to Jesus, a nuance the current definition misses entirely.

audit.author_note: All three occurrences are in Acts (Luke's authorship), so no cross-author variation is detectable; the definition's scope is adequately limited to Acts, but any broader application would be speculative.
